prompt.context: Your firm has won an RFP to help a domestic airline carrier examine their in-flight connectivity (IFC) strategy. With 80% of US-based aircraft already outfitted with IFC technology and competitive pressures rising, offering WiFi service is becoming table-stakes. Your client has yet to enter the game, but they know it's something they need to consider to stay competitive.
prompt.question: What are some of the key things the client should think about when assessing their go-to-market strategy for IFC?

clarifying_info.q: What routes does the airline fly?
clarifying_info.a: The airline flies primarily domestic routes within the continental US, as well as select flights to Canada, Mexico, and the Caribbean.
IFC includes only WiFi connectivity. In-flight entertainment (IFE) is delivered via an on-board server through a separate system, but the two can be integrated into one user experience.

clarifying_info.q: What is the airline's main objective?
clarifying_info.a: The airline's main objective is to stay competitive.

clarifying_info.q: How large is the airline's fleet and how many flights does it operate?
clarifying_info.a: The airline has 90 planes and services approximately 30,000 flights per year.

clarifying_info.q: How is IFC typically installed and managed?
clarifying_info.a: IFC is typically installed and managed by an outside vendor, either through a branded service (e.g., GoGoAir) or a wholesale, white-label solution (e.g., Row44). Contracts are typically 10+ years long.

clarifying_info.q: Do all vendors offer the same technology?
clarifying_info.a: Different vendors use different technologies, which vary in quality.
Total bandwidth is shared across passengers, so the more passengers buy a session, the slower the service. Some carriers intentionally charge high prices to limit usage and ensure better service.

exhibits.title: Competitive Benchmarking
exhibits.shows: A comparison table of two competitor airlines across five dimensions of their IFC business model.

Competitor 1.Airline description: Major domestic and international carrier with 65% fleet IFC coverage

Competitor 2.Airline description: Domestic discount carrier with 90% fleet IFC coverage

exhibits.title: Air Fleet Statistics
exhibits.shows: A table breaking out the client's fleet into wide body and narrow body aircraft with seat counts and annual flight counts.

framework: ROI and/or profitability: will IFC generate positive returns and over what time horizon?
Pricing and business model: free, ad-supported, pay per session, pay per time, pay by speed tier, subscription — and who sets the price?
Market demand: expected take rate by passenger segment, flight type
Costs: upfront CapEx per aircraft, ongoing OpEx (per-session fees, maintenance)
Vendor contract structure: revenue/profit split, investment sharing, branding, contract length, technology quality
Product and user experience: built-in screens vs. BYOD, white-label vs. vendor branding, speeds available, IFE integration, add-on services (calling, texting)
Technology: speed, bandwidth, latency, availability over water
GTM: rollout timing, aircraft prioritization, marketing, crew training, ad sales

questions.prompt: What are your thoughts on the two competitor business models shown in Exhibit 1?
questions.guidance: Candidate should compare the two models using pros and cons. Competitor 1 (vendor-branded, revenue share, $25/session set by vendor): pros include less operational burden on airline, potential for customer experience continuity across carriers (subscriptions), limited costs; cons include limited control over pricing, high price may drive low take rates and anger customers, brand fit concerns. Competitor 2 (airline-branded, wholesale, free): pros include control over pricing and user experience, potential for better ROI, easier IFE integration; cons include more operational burden, higher costs. Candidate should also note: other models exist beyond these two; the exhibit omits critical info such as cost structure, technology quality, product features, and IFE interoperability; it is possible to adopt more than one model across the fleet.

questions.prompt: The client has decided to partner with a white-label IFC vendor to outfit all 90 planes. The airline and vendor will share the initial investment, and the airline will pay the vendor a per-session fee to cover operating expenses. What percentage of passengers need to purchase a session for the airline to break even in 2 years?
questions.guidance: Candidate should request additional data (CapEx per plane, airline's share, margin per session), structure the breakeven equation clearly by aircraft type, and solve for take rate. A strong candidate will also note simplifying assumptions (100% seat occupancy, simultaneous rollout) and react to the resulting take rate in the context of the 5-10% market benchmark.

math.setup: Breakeven requires: Total passengers over 2 years x take rate x margin per session = Total airline investment. CapEx = $250K per plane; airline covers 40%. Margin = $10 per session net of per-session vendor fee.
steps: Airline share of investment per plane: $250K x 40% = $100K
Wide body passengers over 2 yrs: 300 seats x 2,500 flights/yr x 2 yrs = 1,500,000
Narrow body passengers over 2 yrs: 100 seats x 27,500 flights/yr x 2 yrs = 5,500,000
math.answer: ~12.9% take rate required to break even in 2 years

questions.prompt: Market research shows take rates are only 5-10% today for paid connectivity. What do you think are the key drivers of IFC take rate?
questions.guidance: This is a correlation question — what variables correlate with higher take rates? Candidate should brainstorm across multiple buckets and hypothesize the direction each variable must move to drive higher take rate. Strong candidates push into specifics and cover at least three buckets.

brainstorming.prompt: What are the key drivers of IFC take rate?

categories.name: Flight characteristics
ideas: Flight length (longer flights → higher take rate)
Availability of other entertainment systems on board

categories.name: Product characteristics
ideas: Price (lower price → higher take rate, but bandwidth congestion tradeoff)

categories.name: Passenger characteristics
ideas: Age (younger passengers more likely to use WiFi)

recommendation: The airline should partner with a wholesale, white-label vendor to retain control over pricing and the user experience.
Rollout across aircraft should be gradual, potentially starting with a pilot program to optimize pricing, user experience, and vendor performance.
Rollout should prioritize newer planes and routes with the highest expected take rates (e.g., longer flights, high proportion of business travelers).
risks: Due to large upfront investment, the contract is likely to be 10+ years long, making smart vendor selection critical — a vendor agreeing to favorable business model terms may have inferior technology.
Difficult to strike the right balance between maximizing revenue and keeping take rates low enough to preserve service speeds.
IFC technology is still nascent; poor user experience could damage the airline's brand.
next_steps: Conduct detailed vendor selection and contract negotiation.
Develop aircraft prioritization criteria and sequencing plan.
Design and execute a pilot launch to gather data before full fleet rollout.
